Pilar 2 — Physics-Informed ML for Soil Depth Profiles

Hugo Rodrigues

Source: vignettes/pilar2-piml-profile.Rmd
pilar2-piml-profile.Rmd

Abstract

Classical Digital Soil Mapping harmonises horizon observations via equal-area quadratic splines (Bishop et al. 1999; Malone et al. 2009) — a purely mathematical object disconnected from pedogenesis. The Pillar 2 of edaphos replaces that spline with two Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) (Raissi et al. 2019; Karniadakis et al. 2021; Willard et al. 2022) models of the soil depth profile: a parametric pedogenetic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE), solved in closed form and fitted through a horizon-average observation operator, and a Neural ODE (Chen et al. 2018) trained by back-propagation through a fixed-step Runge-Kutta integrator on torch (Falbel and Luraschi 2023). Both models are demonstrated on the aqp::sp4 reference pedons and a hierarchical covariate-conditioned extension closes the loop with Pillar 5.

1. Pedogenetic ODE

Let y(z)y(z) denote a soil property (e.g. clay fraction, SOC) at depth z≥0z\ge 0. The one-dimensional kinetic model of translocation (Jenny 1941; Minasny and McBratney 2016) assumes a depth-dependent relaxation towards an equilibrium coordinate y∞y_{\infty} with rate λ(z)\lambda(z) — a coordinate that, as Section 1 shows below, the solution does not reach: dydz=−λ(z)(y(z)−y∞),λ(z)=λ0e−μz. \frac{dy}{dz}\;=\;-\lambda(z)\,\bigl(y(z)-y_{\infty}\bigr),\qquad \lambda(z)=\lambda_{0}\,e^{-\mu z}. \tag{1} Parameters (λ0,μ,y∞,y0)(\lambda_{0},\mu,y_{\infty},y_{0}) carry explicit physical meaning: λ0\lambda_{0} is the surface pedogenetic rate; μ\mu controls how quickly that rate decays with depth; and y0y_{0} is the surface intercept.

y∞y_{\infty} needs care, because it is not the value the profile reaches. Equation (1) is separable and its solution is y(z)=y∞+(y0−y∞)exp⁡[−λ0μ(1−e−μz)], y(z)=y_{\infty}+(y_{0}-y_{\infty}) \exp\!\Bigl[-\tfrac{\lambda_{0}}{\mu}\bigl(1-e^{-\mu z}\bigr)\Bigr], \tag{2} so, with κ=λ0/μ\kappa=\lambda_{0}/\mu, y(∞)=y∞+(y0−y∞)e−κy(\infty)=y_{\infty}+(y_{0}-y_{\infty})e^{-\kappa}. Because the rate λ(z)\lambda(z) decays with depth, the profile traverses only a fraction 1−e−κ1-e^{-\kappa} of the y0→y∞y_{0}\to y_{\infty} gap and then stops. y∞y_{\infty} is an equilibrium coordinate of the differential equation; the parent-material extrapolation is y(∞)y(\infty), and the two can differ in sign. The fit is carried out in the identified, positive coordinates (y0,y(∞),κ,μ)(y_{0}, y(\infty), \kappa, \mu), with λ0\lambda_{0} and y∞y_{\infty} recovered for reporting. The implementation [piml_profile_fit()][piml_profile_fit] evaluates (2) directly — the equation has a solution, so integrating it numerically is only slower and less accurate — and minimises 𝒥(θ)=∑j(y‾(zjtop,zjbot;θ)−yj)2+η∥θ−θ0∥22, \mathcal{J}(\theta)\;=\; \sum_{j}\bigl(\bar y(z_{j}^{\text{top}},z_{j}^{\text{bot}};\theta)-y_{j}\bigr)^{2} \;+\;\eta\|\theta-\theta_{0}\|_{2}^{2},\tag{3} with Nelder–Mead from several starting points. Two details matter. The forward operator y‾\bar y is the model’s average over the horizon [zjtop,zjbot][z^{\text{top}}_j, z^{\text{bot}}_j], by Gauss–Legendre quadrature on (2), rather than a point evaluation at the mid-depth — a laboratory value is a layer average, which is the same observation-operator issue the equal-area spline literature addresses (Bishop et al. 1999; Malone et al. 2009). And the Tikhonov term is centred on the data-driven start θ0\theta_0: on log coordinates an uncentred penalty shrinks every concentration toward 1, and in earlier versions, applied to the raw y∞y_\infty, it scaled with the square of the property’s units and silently did part of the fitting.1

2. Dataset — aqp::sp4

We use the ten reference pedons of aqp::sp4 with horizon concentrations of clay, sand, Ca, Mg, K, CEC and CF.

data(sp4, package = "aqp")
sp4$depth <- (sp4$top + sp4$bottom) / 2
head(sp4[, c("id", "name", "top", "bottom", "depth", "clay", "K")])
#>       id name top bottom depth clay   K
#> 1 colusa    A   0      3   1.5   21 0.3
#> 2 colusa  ABt   3      8   5.5   27 0.2
#> 3 colusa  Bt1   8     30  19.0   32 0.1
#> 4 colusa  Bt2  30     42  36.0   55 0.1
#> 5  glenn    A   0      9   4.5   25 0.2
#> 6  glenn   Bt   9     34  21.5   34 0.3
unique(sp4$id)
#>  [1] "colusa"         "glenn"          "kings"          "napa"          
#>  [5] "san benito"     "shasta"         "tehama"         "mariposa"      
#>  [9] "mendocino"      "shasta-trinity"

3. Mono-pedon fit: a real multi-horizon profile

Earlier versions of this vignette fitted the napa pedon and called it “a canonical argillic-horizon case … converging to a plateau in the parent material”. It is neither. napa has two horizons, A (0-6 cm) and Bt (6-20 cm), with clay 15% and 17%: two points for a four-parameter model, no plateau to converge to, and no bulge. A monotone increase is not an argillic horizon — an argillic horizon is a clay maximum with depletion above and below it, and equation (1) is monotone by construction, so it cannot represent one at all (Section 4).

We therefore fit a real multi-horizon profile from the WoSIS extract the package ships: 1,105 Cerrado profiles with four or more horizons, built by data-raw/piml_wosis_multihorizon.R from the cached ISRIC WFS layers. Horizon boundaries are known, so the model is matched to the layer average of each horizon rather than to a point at its mid-depth.

W <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "piml_wosis_cerrado.rds",
                         package = "edaphos"))
# the deepest, most completely described profile inside the model's domain
cand <- W$profiles[W$profiles$monotone_decreasing, ]
cand <- cand[order(-cand$n_hor, -cand$z_max), ]
pedon <- W$horizons[W$horizons$profile_id == cand$profile_id[1], ]
pedon <- pedon[order(pedon$top), ]
pedon[, c("top", "bottom", "soc_g_kg")]
#>      top bottom soc_g_kg
#> 6393   0     12     28.9
#> 5704  12     35     17.4
#> 979   35     60     13.6
#> 7216  60    100     10.0
#> 5567 100    150      8.5
#> 842  150    250      6.7
#> 6328 250    350      5.1
#> 6097 350    450      3.7
#> 2565 450    550      2.3

fit_pedon <- piml_profile_fit(
  depths = pedon$depth_mid,
  values = pedon$soc_g_kg,
  top    = pedon$top,
  bottom = pedon$bottom
)
fit_pedon
#> <edaphos_piml_profile>
#>   dy/dz = -lambda0 * exp(-mu*z) * (y - y_inf)
#>   lambda0 = 0.009613  mu = 0.004151
#>   y0      = 23.45     y(Inf) = 1.982      (kappa = 2.32)
#>   y_inf   = -0.3678   (ODE coordinate, not the attained value)
#>   n obs   = 9 (layer)         rmse = 2.517
#>   converged = TRUE

The printed object separates two things the package used to conflate: y(Inf), the value the profile actually reaches, and y_inf, a coordinate of the differential equation that it does not. It also reports kappa, the fraction of the journey the profile completes.

grid_z <- seq(0, max(pedon$bottom) * 1.1, by = 1)
pred_pedon <- data.frame(depth = grid_z,
                         soc   = predict(fit_pedon, grid_z))
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = pred_pedon, aes(soc, depth),
            linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(data = pedon, aes(soc_g_kg, depth_mid),
             size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(fit_pedon$params),
             linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Organic carbon (g kg"^-1, ")")),
       y = "Depth (cm)",
       title = "A real WoSIS profile and the fitted pedogenetic ODE",
       subtitle = "dashed line: y(Inf), the value the solution actually reaches") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

4. Multi-pedon diagnostics

Fitting the full sp4 dataset recovers an interpretable table where every row has a direct pedological meaning.

fits <- piml_profile_fit_group(
  sp4, id = "id", depth = "depth", value = "clay"
)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fits), function(k) {
  p <- fits[[k]]$params
  data.frame(
    pedon   = k,
    lambda0  = signif(p$lambda0, 3),
    mu       = signif(p$mu,      3),
    kappa    = signif(p$kappa,   3),
    y0       = signif(p$y0,      3),
    # the value the profile reaches -- NOT y_inf, which is reported
    # alongside it to show how far apart the two can be
    y_attain = signif(edaphos:::.piml_asymptote(p), 3),
    y_inf    = signif(p$y_inf,   3),
    rmse     = signif(fits[[k]]$rmse, 3)
  )
}))
tab
#>                     pedon lambda0      mu   kappa     y0 y_attain y_inf
#> log_kappa          colusa 0.00441 0.00333  1.3200 19.900    181.0 239.0
#> log_kappa1          glenn 0.05900 0.02330  2.5400 20.100     40.3  42.1
#> log_kappa2          kings 0.03210 0.00887  3.6200  0.124     52.1  53.5
#> log_kappa3       mariposa 1.02000 0.01210 84.0000 40.800     29.5  29.5
#> log_kappa4      mendocino 0.42000 0.03680 11.4000  7.870     23.1  23.1
#> log_kappa5           napa 0.10100 0.03860  2.6100 13.800     18.4  18.8
#> log_kappa6     san benito 0.07720 0.03080  2.5100  6.750     26.0  27.7
#> log_kappa7         shasta 0.00010 0.02330  0.0043 14.000     14.0  14.0
#> log_kappa8 shasta-trinity 0.02500 0.01530  1.6400 18.700    102.0 123.0
#> log_kappa9         tehama 0.01680 0.02560  0.6560 21.800     50.9  82.2
#>                rmse
#> log_kappa  3.55e+00
#> log_kappa1 1.35e-02
#> log_kappa2 1.72e+00
#> log_kappa3 2.95e+00
#> log_kappa4 8.20e-02
#> log_kappa5 3.17e-03
#> log_kappa6 2.80e-02
#> log_kappa7 3.55e-15
#> log_kappa8 1.58e+00
#> log_kappa9 1.03e+00

Read this table with y_attain — the value the profile reaches — and not y_inf. On colusa and tehama the two differ by orders of magnitude, and both are absurd: those pedons have three or four horizons, all in the top 42 cm, with clay still rising at the deepest one. There is simply no information in them about where the argillic horizon levels off, so the curve is fitted through the observations and then points off to nowhere. print() flags exactly these two, reporting how far down the y0→y(∞)y_0 \to y(\infty) journey the deepest horizon actually got:

vapply(fits, function(f) f$progress, numeric(1))
#>         colusa          glenn          kings       mariposa      mendocino 
#>      0.1893752      0.6859613      0.5464827      1.0000000      0.9967878 
#>           napa     san benito         shasta shasta-trinity         tehama 
#>      0.6933642      0.6361349      1.0000000      0.5770621      0.3204463

On neither flagged pedon does the four-parameter equation improve on a two-parameter straight line (next section: 3.018 against 3.016, and 0.839 against 0.836), which is the right outcome — the model should not be credited for a shape it did not determine.

5. Non-physical baselines

Two baselines bound the improvement claim: the mean predictor and the linear-in-depth regression. A meaningful PIML gain should come from the physical constraint, not from extra parameters.

baseline_rmse <- function(sub, target) {
  y <- sub[[target]]
  c(mean   = sqrt(mean((y - mean(y))^2)),
    linear = sqrt(mean(stats::residuals(
                     stats::lm(y ~ sub$depth))^2)))
}
bench <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(sp4, sp4$id), function(sub) {
  bl <- baseline_rmse(sub, "clay")
  data.frame(pedon = sub$id[1],
             piml  = fits[[sub$id[1]]]$rmse,
             mean_baseline = bl["mean"],
             linear_baseline = bl["linear"])
}))
bench
#>                         pedon         piml mean_baseline linear_baseline
#> colusa                 colusa 3.548319e+00     12.871966       3.0163775
#> glenn                   glenn 1.352830e-02      4.500000       0.0000000
#> kings                   kings 1.718484e+00      9.797959       2.5628166
#> mariposa             mariposa 2.949986e+00      3.112475       2.7467763
#> mendocino           mendocino 8.202878e-02      4.320494       2.5935243
#> napa                     napa 3.165961e-03      1.000000       0.0000000
#> san benito         san benito 2.799550e-02      3.500000       0.0000000
#> shasta                 shasta 3.552714e-15      0.000000       0.0000000
#> shasta-trinity shasta-trinity 1.575534e+00     16.697305       3.0480840
#> tehama                 tehama 1.034476e+00      3.559026       0.8360796

6. Neural ODE variant

For profiles where the mono-asymptotic prior is violated — illuviated bulges, E horizons beneath A, buried paleosols — edaphos offers a Neural ODE alternative (Chen et al. 2018): dydz=fθ(z,y),fθ=MLP(z,y;θ). \frac{dy}{dz}=f_{\theta}(z,y),\qquad f_{\theta}=\text{MLP}(z,y;\,\theta). \tag{4} The forward map is a fixed-step RK4 integrator written directly in torch, so training back-propagates the squared-error loss through the whole trajectory: 𝒥NODE(θ)=∑j(∫0zjfθ(z,y(z))dz+y0⏟RK4 rollout−yj)2. \mathcal{J}_{\text{NODE}}(\theta) \;=\;\sum_{j}\Bigl( \underbrace{\int_{0}^{z_{j}}f_{\theta}(z,y(z))\,dz +y_{0}}_{\text{RK4 rollout}} \;-\;y_{j}\Bigr)^{2}. 

nn_fit <- piml_neural_ode_fit(
  depths  = pedon$depth_mid, values = pedon$soc_g_kg,
  hidden  = c(16L, 16L), epochs = 500L,
  seed    = 1L, verbose = FALSE
)
nn_fit
pred_nn <- data.frame(depth = grid_z,
                      soc   = predict(nn_fit, grid_z))
ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = pred_pedon, aes(soc, depth,
            colour = "Parametric ODE"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = pred_nn,   aes(soc, depth,
            colour = "Neural ODE"),     linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = pedon, aes(soc_g_kg, depth_mid),
             size = 3, colour = "firebrick") +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Parametric ODE" = "steelblue",
                                  "Neural ODE"    = "darkgreen")) +
  labs(x = expression(paste("Organic carbon (g kg"^-1, ")")),
       y = "Depth (cm)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Parametric vs. Neural ODE on the same real profile") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

7. Pillar 2 × Pillar 5 — the physics gate

Given a PIML fit (parametric or neural), the helper [al_physics_gate_piml()][al_physics_gate_piml] constructs a rejection function: candidates whose predicted target falls outside the range the solution actually spans, [min⁡(y0,y(∞)),max⁡(y0,y(∞))][\min(y_{0},y(\infty)),\,\max(y_{0},y(\infty))], inflated by a safety_factor, are eliminated from the greedy Active-Learning selection (see the Pillar 5 vignette). The envelope used to be built from y∞y_{\infty}, which is not a value any profile reaches and is often negative: on 300 real WoSIS pedons the gate then accepted an organic carbon of −5-5 g/kg on 73 of them. It now floors at zero for a property the fit itself requires to be positive.

gate <- al_physics_gate_piml(fit_pedon, safety_factor = 1.2)
cand_dummy <- data.frame(dummy = 1:4)
gate(cand_dummy, predicted_mean = c(10, 25, 200, -5))

A hierarchical extension ([piml_hierarchical_fit()][piml_hierarchical_fit]) jointly fits a covariate-conditioned Neural ODE across pedons, delivering a per-location envelope that [al_physics_gate_piml_hierarchical()][al_physics_gate_piml_hierarchical] feeds back into Pillar 5.

8. Bayesian posterior over the ODE parameters

[piml_profile_fit()][piml_profile_fit] returns a single point estimate. For any honest downstream use — propagating parametric uncertainty into a SOC-stock prediction, tuning a Pillar 5 Active-Learning acquisition under correct epistemic variance, reporting publishable parameter intervals — we need the posterior p(λ0,μ,y∞,y0∣depths,values)p(\lambda_0, \mu, y_\infty, y_0 \mid \text{depths}, \text{values}), not just the MAP.

The function [piml_profile_fit_bayesian()][piml_profile_fit_bayesian] returns that posterior through two nested approximations:

  1. Laplace approximation (default, O(ms) per pedon). Gaussian posterior whose mean is the MAP and whose covariance is the inverse observed Fisher information at the MAP (Bishop 2006, sec. 4.4). Accurate when the posterior is well-identified; every call pre-samples 2 000 draws from N(MAP,Σ)N(\text{MAP}, \Sigma) for predictive convenience.
  2. Adaptive random-walk Metropolis (Haario et al. 2001) (~seconds per pedon). Proposal covariance starts at the Laplace covariance, scaled by the Roberts–Gelman–Gilks optimal factor (2.38)2/d(2.38)^2 / d, and is updated online by Haario recursion after a warm-up period — so non-Gaussian or multimodal posteriors are captured faithfully where Laplace would paper over them.

Which to use, measured rather than asserted. On the WoSIS pedon the manuscript reports (1115679, nine horizons to 550 cm, lognormal family, horizon-average operator, same seed), the two paths were compared parameter by parameter. Five of the seven 95% intervals are narrower under Laplace — κ\kappa and y∞y_\infty by more than a factor of two, the observation noise by 1.8, so its coefficient of variation reads 0.168 against 0.230 from the sampler.

The split is not arbitrary. The attainable deep value y(∞)y(\infty), which these data identify, is essentially unchanged (width ratio 1.01), and μ\mu is actually wider under Laplace. What moves is what is not identified. The derived y∞=(A−y0e−κ)/(1−e−κ)y_\infty = (A - y_0 e^{-\kappa})/(1 - e^{-\kappa}) has a pole at κ→0\kappa \to 0; the sampler puts 5.3% of its draws below κ=0.5\kappa = 0.5 and reaches 0.080, while Laplace puts 0.5% there and stops at 0.285. Conditioning both on κ≥0.5\kappa \ge 0.5 brings them into agreement.

So the practical rule is the one the description above already implies, now with a measurement behind it: Laplace is fine for the identified coordinates and for anything you intend to use as a point estimate, and it is not fine for a derived quantity whose map is unstable in a tail it cannot reach. The package’s reported numbers use MCMC.

library(edaphos)

depths <- c(5, 15, 30, 60, 100)
values <- c(25, 18, 12, 8, 6.5)

fit_bayes <- piml_profile_fit_bayesian(depths, values,
                                         method = "laplace", seed = 1L)
fit_bayes
#> <edaphos_piml_bayes>
#>   method     : laplace
#>   n draws    : 2000
#>   sigma (noise): 0.009692
#>   posterior summary (natural scale):
#>  parameter      mean        sd       q2.5       q50    q97.5
#>    lambda0   0.03740  0.012180   0.018942  0.035352  0.06675
#>         mu   0.03509  0.005514   0.025552  0.034733  0.04736
#>      y_inf -10.64234 11.818452 -41.257663 -8.089489  3.62039
#>         y0  30.98891  0.602453  29.837477 31.006206 32.15824
#>      kappa   1.14603  0.571184   0.399185  1.016122  2.59166
#>     y_asym   6.05674  0.177663   5.707088  6.056401  6.41648
#>      sigma   0.01029  0.003757   0.004745  0.009672  0.01924
predict(fit_bayes,
         newdepths         = c(10, 20, 40, 80),
         interval          = 0.95,
         include_obs_noise = TRUE,
         seed              = 1L)
#>   depth      mean        sd     lower     upper lower_sim upper_sim
#> 1    10 20.589711 0.5581681 19.319254 21.293824 18.788348 21.458065
#> 2    20 15.054671 0.5770224 13.482066 15.709122 12.862055 15.794151
#> 3    40  9.883594 0.3760792  8.874115 10.306881  8.553220 10.379022
#> 4    80  6.905800 0.1433822  6.555402  7.121222  6.436077  7.160627

include_obs_noise = TRUE adds Gaussian observation noise with the MAP-estimated σ\sigma onto every predictive draw, so the returned interval represents the predictive distribution of a future observation rather than the uncertainty on the mean function alone.

For the Neural-ODE variant the variational analogue is a deep ensemble (Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017): K independent networks trained from different random seeds produce an empirical posterior whose mean and variance approximate the Bayesian predictive posterior (Wilson and Izmailov 2020).

ens <- piml_neural_ode_fit_ensemble(depths, values,
                                       K = 5L, epochs = 300L, seed = 1L)
predict(ens, newdepths = c(10, 20, 40, 80), interval = 0.9)

9. Discussion and roadmap

The parametric ODE is mono-asymptotic and therefore optimal for properties that decay monotonically toward a parent-material value (SOC, some nutrients) but suboptimal for bimodal profiles, which the Neural ODE handles by construction. Three complementary directions remain on the roadmap:

  • Mass-conservation soft constraints — augment the Neural ODE loss with a term penalising deviations from an integrated mass balance (Minasny et al. 2017).
  • Adjoint-method Neural ODE — for pedons deeper than 2 m, the back-propagation graph becomes memory-bound; the adjoint method of (Chen et al. 2018) eliminates that scaling.
  • Hierarchical Bayesian pooling — extending [piml_hierarchical_fit()][piml_hierarchical_fit] to the posterior regime that [piml_profile_fit_bayesian()][piml_profile_fit_bayesian] already exposes for single pedons, with covariate-conditioned priors over (λ0,μ,y∞,y0)(\lambda_0, \mu, y_\infty, y_0).
